title: Loktak: The Lake That Breathes
subtitle: Stories of a floating world and a deer that walks on water
era: Living wetland history, ancient traditions to the 21st century
region: Loktak Lake, Moirang and Keibul Lamjao, Manipur
moral: The wisest engineering can be alive, seasonal and humble.

sources.citation: Ramsar Convention designation for Loktak Lake, 23 March 1990, and Montreux Record listing, 16 June 1993
sources.note: Official primary conservation records for the threatened wetland.

sources.citation: Loktak Development Authority technical reports and Keibul Lamjao National Park records
sources.note: Primary administrative sources on phumdi, water management and the Sangai habitat.

sources.citation: Cheitharol Kumbaba references to Moirang, boat races and valley water culture, in Parratt (2005)
sources.note: Historical context for Manipur's lake and water traditions.

panels.shot: wide aerial dusk shot over a mosaic of floating phumdi, with a lone deer and a fisher in frame

dialogue.text: On Loktak, houses float, deer walk on water, and a whole people balance between hunger and flood. This is the living story of the lake that breathes.

panels.shot: slow push-in from above onto the lake surface transforming with seasons

dialogue.text: Year after year, Loktak grows and shrinks with the sky. The water climbs into fields, then retreats, leaving thick mats of roots and reeds drifting like islands.

panels.shot: medium shot at water level, focused on hands lifting phumdi

dialogue.text: The people of Moirang learned to read this breathing lake. They cut and shaped the drifting phumdi, turning wild plant mats into tools, fields and shelter.

panels.shot: wide tranquil dawn shot showing phumshang settlement

dialogue.text: On these living rafts they raised phumshang huts. Floors of woven bamboo, walls of thatch, all resting on floating earth that sways when a child runs or a storm kicks the waves.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of circular athapum structures in the lake

dialogue.text: They built athapum—floating rings that lure fish into a quiet trap. No stone embankments, no iron gates. Just reeds, roots and patience, drifting where the fish and currents move.

panels.shot: low wide shot of boat race from the shoreline perspective

dialogue.text: Court chronicles like the Cheitharol Kumbaba remember Moirang for its boats and water games. For valley kings, these waters were pride and power; for fishers, they were bread and breath.

panels.shot: medium shot under overcast sky, fisher adjusting a net, hills in background

dialogue.text: No inscription dates the first phumshang. The record is the living routine: nets at dawn, offerings to the water, stories of storms that carried away homes and of returns to rebuild on the same drifting ground.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Sangai on phumdi with fisher in the distant background

dialogue.text: On the southern fringe lies Keibul Lamjao, the world’s only floating national park. Here the Sangai, Manipur’s brow-antlered deer, steps softly on phumdi that shifts under each careful hoof.

panels.shot: tight shot of fisher’s face watching a distant Sangai at sunset

dialogue.speaker: the_fisherfolk_of_loktak
dialogue.text: If the phumdi sinks, both our lives go under.

panels.shot: archival-style montage shot with split frame: old and new

dialogue.text: Then came concrete and control. Ithai barrage held the waters high for power and irrigation, but the lake that once rose and fell with the seasons was pinned to a new rhythm.

panels.shot: medium shot from bank showing raised waterline against trees and homesteads

dialogue.text: Reports note what the eye already saw. Higher water levels buried fields, changed fish routes, and kept phumdi afloat longer on the surface instead of resting on the lakebed in dry months.

panels.shot: wide shot of Keibul Lamjao showing thinning phumdi and concerned figures in distance

dialogue.text: Scientists and lake dwellers watched the Sangai’s ground soften. With altered water regimes, phumdi in the park thinned and shifted, its weight and thickness no longer following the old cycle of sinking and rising.

panels.shot: documentary-style medium shot of fisher at a meeting with officials, maps behind

dialogue.text: The lake became a meeting table. Fishers spoke of rights and eviction, officials of weed control and power, conservationists of Sangai numbers and water quality. The same water lay behind every argument.

panels.shot: insert shot of official documents and a globe, with Loktak in focus

dialogue.text: In 1990, the Ramsar Convention listed Loktak as a wetland of international importance. In 1993, it entered the Montreux Record, named among sites where change had placed the ecosystem under strain.

panels.shot: wide shot of lake showing both pollution and traditional activity

dialogue.text: Pollution flowed from towns, pesticides from fields, silt from hills. Yet among this, phumdi still held up huts and nets, and the lake people still turned floating weed into food and income.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot inside a phumshang at night

dialogue.speaker: the_fisherfolk_of_loktak
dialogue.text: The reports write our lake, but they do not feel this sway.

panels.shot: sunrise wide shot of fisher and Sangai sharing the landscape

dialogue.text: The fisher and the deer remain tied to the same floating earth, each step testing the strength of the mat beneath, each season waiting to see how the lake will choose to breathe next.

panels.shot: lingering high-angle shot over Loktak showing mosaic of human and wild spaces

dialogue.text: Loktak’s story asks a quiet question: can our grand engineering learn from this modest craft, where infrastructure floats, yields and adjusts, and survival depends on listening to a lake that still breathes?
